title: feat(realtime): support Gemini 3.8 Live Extended Thinking
body:
## AgentScope Version

2.0.12dev

## Description

> The review fixes below are implemented and validated in the local working
> tree, but have not yet been committed/pushed. Validation below is local and
> does not claim CI coverage of the current remote head.

Add Gemini 3.8 Live Extended Thinking with configurable reasoning levels and
non-blocking tools. Keep spoken fillers, tool calls, and follow-up output in one
logical reply. Preserve user transcription order when it arrives after a tool
continuation, including frames that contain output or only `IN_PROGRESS`.

The Thinking model uses the **v1alpha WebSocket endpoint** and interaction-status
completion instead of treating every `turnComplete` as the end of a reply.
Its card explicitly enables `supports_extended_thinking`, so aliases and custom
cards select the same endpoint and tool/lifecycle semantics. Ordinary Live
models retain their existing protocol mode.

When a user interrupts, cancel pending confirmations and retain completed tool
results in the original reply. Late Extended Thinking results use
`functionResponse.scheduling: SILENT`, preserving provider context without
requesting fresh output or disturbing a newer reply's follow-up bookkeeping.
Across **all Gemini Live models**, tool results in `ERROR`, `DENIED`, or
`INTERRUPTED` state now use `response.error` instead of `response.output`.
This wire-format change also applies to Gemini 3.8 Live, Gemini 3.1 Flash Live
Preview, and Gemini 2.5 Flash Native Audio; it is not restricted to Thinking.
Silent scheduling remains exclusive to Extended Thinking's non-blocking tools.
Stale confirmations produce a warning without authorizing another reply's tool.

The public API additions are backward-compatible and require no changes to
existing adapter implementations:

- `RealtimeModelBase.start_turn()` reports a local VAD speech boundary so
  adapters can settle input independently of response cancellation.
- `RealtimeModelBase.push_tool_result_silently()` delegates to the existing
  result method by default. Providers whose tool results implicitly trigger
  generation can override it; Gemini implements silent scheduling for
  non-blocking Extended Thinking tools. The existing `push_tool_result()`
  signature is unchanged.
- `RealtimeModelCard.supports_extended_thinking` is a public capability field
  defaulting to `False`. Gemini derives its endpoint, non-blocking declarations,
  and interaction-status semantics from the card instead of a model-name match.

Also process setup acknowledgments before content/status early returns, retain
both status placements documented in the Thinking guide, and add sourced model
metadata. The advertised 900-second audio session limit applies without context
window compression.

## Validation

Regression coverage includes interruption while confirming or executing a tool,
late results after a new reply starts, silent result scheduling, successful and
failed tool payloads, custom-card aliases, setup acknowledgment in mixed frames,
confirmation ownership, and transcription/checkpoint/reconnect ordering.

In `agentscope2`, the latest Gemini suite passed **29 tests and 73 subtests**.
Its tool-result matrix covers all four shipped Gemini cards, all five result
states, and normal/silent delivery: **40 combinations**. It asserts the full
payload, including `error` for failures and no `scheduling` on non-Thinking
models.

The Agent suite passed during the preceding review-fix validation, as did the
other realtime provider, delegation, checkpoint, service, reconnect, and WebRTC
suites (139 tests and 59 subtests). This follow-up changes tests and description
only. Tests use actual adapters with mocked transports; no live-provider session
has been run.

All applicable pre-commit hooks passed for the changed files, including mypy,
Black, Flake8, and Pylint. `git diff --check` also passed.

Silent scheduling does not cancel provider output that was already in flight;
ordinary blocking Live tools retain their existing scheduling behavior, with
the error-encoding change described above.

title: fix(tool): skip a PowerShell candidate that cannot run
body:
## Problem

`PowerShell._resolve_executable()` probes each candidate shell with
`exit 0` and caches the first one that is not "not found":

```python
probe = await self._backend.exec_shell([...], timeout=10.0)
if probe.exit_code != 127:
    self._executable = candidate
    break
```

The backend reports a probe that was killed — by that 10 s timeout — as
`exit_code == -1` (`ExecResult(exit_code=-1, ..., stderr=b"timed out")`),
and `-1 != 127` passes the test. A `pwsh` that exists on `PATH` but
cannot start (broken install, binary on an unreachable network share, a
stalled WSL bridge) is therefore cached as **the** shell for the rest of
the process, and every later command fails or waits out its timeout
instead of falling back to `powershell.exe`, which is present and works.

The probe runs `exit 0`, so anything but a zero exit says the candidate
could not be used.

## Fix

```python
if probe.exit_code == 0:
    self._executable = candidate
    break
```

A probe that exits 127 (not found) or -1 (killed) falls through to the
next candidate. If none of them answers, the existing `else` branch
still falls back to `powershell.exe`, so the tool never ends up without
a shell.

## Test

`test_probe_that_cannot_run_falls_back_to_the_next_shell`
(`tests/builtin_powershell_test.py`): a mocked backend answers the
`pwsh` probe with `ExecResult(-1, b"", b"timed out")` and the
`powershell.exe` probe with `ExecResult(0, b"", b"")`; the test asserts
the resolved shell is `powershell.exe`, that it is cached (the second
call probes nothing), and that exactly two probes ran.

Verified with the source fix reverted: the test fails with
`'pwsh' != 'powershell.exe'`. With the fix,
`tests/builtin_powershell_test.py` passes (16 tests, including the real
PowerShell execution cases on Windows).

title: fix(memory): start the ReMe app once for concurrent callers
body:
## Problem

`ReMeMiddleware._ensure_started()` is documented as idempotent ("started
once (idempotent guards)"), but the check has no lock:

```python
if self._app is None:
    self._app = self._build_app()
if not self._started:
    ... await self._app.update_component(...)
    await self._app.start()
    self._started = True
```

The middleware is shared by every agent that uses it, and every hook
awaits this method. Two hooks that run concurrently on a fresh
middleware — two users' first messages, or one agent's retrieve and
write-back paths — both observe `_started == False`, both `await`
`update_component()` and both call `start()` on the embedded ReMe app.
Measured with a fake app whose `start()` yields:

```
start calls: 5   (5 concurrent callers)
```

Starting ReMe twice re-runs its component initialisation and can leave
two stores/indexes alive behind one app.

## Fix

Serialize the one-time start with an `asyncio.Lock` and re-check
`_started` under it (double-checked locking), so the app is built,
configured and started exactly once even when many callers arrive
together. The lock is released if `start()` raises, so a later call can
still retry.

## Test

`test_concurrent_callers_start_the_app_once`
(`tests/reme_middleware_test.py`, new `TestAppLifecycle`): patches
`_build_app` with a fake whose `start()` yields, runs five
`_ensure_started()` calls with `asyncio.gather`, and asserts
`start_count == 1`, `_started is True` and `_app` is that fake.

Verified with the source fix reverted: the test fails with `5 != 1`.
With the fix, `tests/reme_middleware_test.py` passes (36 tests).

title: fix(agent): copy the context config before applying the deprecated buffer override
body:
## Problem

`InjectionConfig.context_buffer_ratio` is deprecated in favour of
`ContextConfig.context_buffer_ratio`, and `Agent.__init__` applies it with
a direct write:

```python
self.context_config.context_buffer_ratio = (
    self.injection_config.context_buffer_ratio
)
```

`context_config` is whatever object the caller passed in. A caller that
builds one `ContextConfig` and shares it between several agents — a
template config, or a factory returning a cached instance — gets it
mutated: every other agent constructed with that object silently inherits
the deprecated value, including agents created *before* the override, and
the caller's own config no longer matches what it configured. Pydantic
models are validated but not copied on assignment, so nothing protects
the shared instance.

## Fix

Copy the config before applying the deprecated override:

```python
self.context_config = self.context_config.model_copy(deep=True)
self.context_config.context_buffer_ratio = ...
```

Both the deprecation path and the caller's object keep their original
values; the new agent still sees the requested ratio.

## Test

`test_deprecated_override_does_not_mutate_the_caller_config` in
`tests/agent_basic_test.py` builds one `ContextConfig` with a ratio of
`0.2`, constructs an agent with the deprecated
`InjectionConfig(context_buffer_ratio=0.5)`, and constructs a second agent
with the same config object afterwards. It asserts the overriding agent
uses `0.5` while the caller's object and the second agent both stay at
`0.2`.

Verified with the source fix reverted: `AssertionError: 0.5 != 0.2`; with
the fix, all 19 tests in the file pass.

title: fix(scheduler): authorize schedule deletes before removing the job
body:
## Problem

`ScheduleDelete.__call__` removed the in-process APScheduler job *before*
asking storage to delete the record:

```python
try:
    self._scheduler.remove_job(schedule_id)
except JobLookupError:
    pass

deleted = await session_service.delete_schedule(self._user_id, schedule_id)

if not deleted:
    return ToolChunk(... "ScheduleNotFoundError" ..., ERROR)
```

`SessionService.delete_schedule()` reports `False` whenever the row is
not stored under the caller's user id, so another user's `schedule_id`
(or any failed storage delete) takes the owner's timer off the live
scheduler while returning an error to the caller. The record survives,
but `SchedulerManager._reconcile_locked()` skips it:

```python
if self._versions.get(schedule_id) == record.updated_at:
    continue
```

`_versions` is only written by `_add_job()` and popped by
`_remove_job()`; the direct `self._scheduler.remove_job()` bypasses both,
so the version still matches and reconciliation never re-registers the
job. The schedule silently stops firing until the process restarts or
the record is edited.

## Fix

Perform the storage delete first, and remove the scheduler job only
after it reports the record was actually deleted. The best-effort
`JobLookupError` handling is unchanged.

## Test

`test_unauthorized_delete_keeps_the_owner_timer` stores a record under
user `owner`, lets the enabled manager register its timer, and calls
`ScheduleDelete` built for user `intruder`. It asserts the tool returns
`ERROR`, the record is still present, and the job id is still in the
scheduler.

Verified with the source fix reverted: the test fails because the job
was removed (`[]` instead of `[record.id]`); with the fix it passes, and
the full scheduler suite passes (20 tests, 10 subtests).

title: fix(app): fail wakeup startup when the subscription breaks early
body:
## Problem

`WakeupDispatcher.__aenter__` starts the listener and waits for its
`on_ready` callback before publishing the startup signal:

```python
self._task = asyncio.create_task(self._loop(ready), ...)
await ready.wait()
```

`_loop` catches every exception from `subscribe` and returns, but it has
no `finally` that sets `ready`:

```python
try:
    async for _signal in self._bus.subscribe(..., on_ready=ready.set):
        await self._drain_and_dispatch()
except Exception:
    logger.exception("WakeupDispatcher loop crashed; subscription ended.")
```

If `subscribe()` raises *before* invoking `on_ready` — a Redis connection
error while establishing the pub/sub subscription is the common case —
the listener is already gone, `ready` is never set, and application
startup blocks on `ready.wait()` forever. The task stays pending until
the process is killed; the `if self._task.done(): raise RuntimeError(...)`
check a few lines later is unreachable in this path. Sibling loops
(`IndexTaskConsumer._loop`, `CancelDispatcher._loop`) already set the
event in a `finally` block for exactly this reason.

## Fix

Set `ready` in a `finally` block so `__aenter__` always reaches its
existing "subscription ended during startup" check, which raises
`RuntimeError` and cleans up the started tasks instead of hanging.

## Test

`test_startup_fails_when_subscription_raises_before_ready` patches the
bus with a `subscribe` that raises `ConnectionError("broker down")`
immediately, then awaits `__aenter__` with a 1 s timeout and expects a
`RuntimeError` mentioning the subscription, with `_task` and
`_fallback_task` cleared.

Verified with the source fix reverted: the test times out waiting inside
`__aenter__` at `await ready.wait()` (1 failed); with the fix it passes,
and the rest of the dispatcher suite still passes (75 tests across the
wakeup and scheduler files).

title: fix(realtime): release streams when local transport start fails
body:
## Problem

`LocalAudioTransport.start()` creates and starts the input stream and then
the output stream. If the output stream fails to be created or started
(for example, the output device is busy), the exception propagates out of
`start()`. `TransportBase.__aenter__` only calls `close()` when `start()`
returns normally, so the already-started microphone stream is never
stopped: the device stays open for the lifetime of the process and a later
`start()` can fail with "device already in use".

## Fix

Wrap the stream creation and both `start()` calls in a `try/except
BaseException` block. On failure, stop and close whichever streams were
created (best effort), reset `_in_stream`, `_out_stream` and `_loop` to
their idle values, and re-raise the original exception.

## Test

`test_start_failure_releases_open_streams` enters the transport with
`async with` and a fake `sounddevice` whose `OutputStream.start` raises
`RuntimeError`. It asserts that both streams are stopped and closed once
and that the transport is back to its idle state.

Verified with the source fix reverted: the new test fails because
`in_stream.stop()` is never called; with the fix it passes. The full
`tests/realtime_local_transport_test.py` file passes (8 tests).

title: fix(app): ignore duplicate index tasks for ready documents
body:
## AgentScope Version

2.0.12dev

## Description

Fixes #3650.

`IndexWorker.process` guards concurrent work with a processing lease, but that lease only excludes workers that are indexing *right now*. Once a delivery reaches `ready` it releases the lease, so a duplicate entry in the durable index queue acquires a fresh lease and runs the whole pipeline again. Because the pipeline calls `delete_document` before generating new embeddings, a transient failure on that second run destroys chunks that were already healthy and leaves the document in `error`, with no reindex requested by anyone.

This adds an admission check at the top of `_run_pipeline`: a document whose status is already `ready` is skipped, so a duplicate delivery does nothing at all.

The check is deliberately narrow. `error` is **not** treated as terminal, so a redelivery of a failed document is still reprocessed, and an explicit re-index keeps working through the existing status reset to `pending`. The scope matches the expected behaviour recorded in the issue.

**Tests** (`tests/index_worker_duplicate_task_test.py`, real `IndexWorker` over storage, blob and vector-store doubles):

- a delivery after `ready` leaves status, chunk count, recorded transitions, embedding calls and vector-store writes exactly as they were
- a failing embedding backend cannot degrade a `ready` document through a duplicate delivery — this is the reported damage, and on unmodified `main` it ends in `error` with zero chunks
- ignoring a duplicate still releases the lease it acquired
- a `pending` document is still indexed normally
- an `error` document is still re-indexed

Also adds the top-level `status` field to the record stub in `tests/index_worker_content_type_test.py`; the pipeline now reads it, and `KnowledgeDocumentRecord` really does carry it at the top level.

Verified locally: the two defect tests fail on unmodified `main` and pass with the fix, the three "real work still runs" tests pass on both, and on the pristine base the two defect tests fail and every other test in `index_worker_lease_test`, `index_worker_main_test` and `index_worker_content_type_test` passes unchanged (6 passed + 2 subtests before and after), and the failure set of `rag_parser_test` and `service_enqueue_index_task_test` is byte-identical before and after (71, all pre-existing: `rag_parser` needs optional document backends and the enqueue tests need a Redis that answers `eval`, neither of which works on this Windows box -- both reproduce on an untouched checkout of the base commit). `black`, `flake8`, `pylint` (10.00/10) and `mypy` are clean on the touched files; the rest is left to CI.

title: fix(permission): treat TaskList/TaskGet as read-only so EXPLORE allows them
body:
## Problem

In `EXPLORE` (plan) mode, `TaskList` and `TaskGet` are **denied**, although both only read task state. Only `TaskCreate` / `TaskUpdate` modify anything, yet all four inherit the same verdict.

## Root cause

`_TaskToolBase` hard-codes

```python
is_read_only: bool = False
```

which is correct for the two writers and wrong for the two readers. `TaskList.call` and `TaskGet.call` only iterate `_agent_state.tasks_context.tasks`.

The base class tries to compensate with its own permission hook:

```python
async def check_permissions(self, tool_input, context) -> PermissionDecision:
    return PermissionDecision(behavior=PermissionBehavior.ALLOW, message="... always allowed ...")
```

but `EXPLORE` never consults the tool: per `permission/_engine.py`, step 4 of `_check_explore` is *"`tool.check_permissions` → not applicable"* — the mode is fully resolved by the read-only verdict. So both readers fall through to the mode's final DENY, contradicting the documented `PermissionMode.EXPLORE` contract (*"Allow: read-only tools … Deny: any modification tool"*).

## Change

Mark the two readers read-only:

- `src/agentscope/tool/_task/_list_task.py`: `TaskList.is_read_only = True`
- `src/agentscope/tool/_task/_get_task.py`: `TaskGet.is_read_only = True`

`TaskCreate` / `TaskUpdate` keep the inherited `False`, so `EXPLORE` still denies them, and `DEFAULT` / `ACCEPT_EDITS` behaviour for the readers improves consistently (they are now recognised as read-only there too).

## Verification

Two tests added to `PermissionEngineExploreModeTest` in `tests/permission_mode_test.py`:

- `test_explore_task_readers_allow` — `TaskList()` and `TaskGet()` → `ALLOW`;
- `test_explore_task_writers_deny` — `TaskCreate()` and `TaskUpdate()` → `DENY` (guards against over-correcting).

```
uv run python -m pytest tests/permission_mode_test.py -q
with the change:                     30 passed, 24 skipped
with the two task files reverted:     1 failed, 29 passed
```

The failure without the change is the reported behaviour:

```
AssertionError: <PermissionBehavior.DENY: 'deny'> != <PermissionBehavior.ALLOW: 'allow'>
```

Related suites:

```
uv run python -m pytest tests/permission_mode_test.py tests/task_tool_test.py tests/toolkit_task_test.py -q
63 passed, 24 skipped

uv run ruff check <changed files> → All checks passed!
```

## Note on how this was produced

Produced with an AI coding agent (DeepSeek Harness, model `deepseek-v4.1-flash`, autonomous mode); the human account holder is submitting and will respond to review comments.

Closes #3567

title: fix(permission): await a decorated async match_rule instead of failing open
body:
## Problem

The permission system **fails open** when a tool's async `match_rule` is wrapped by an ordinary sync decorator (`functools.wraps` over an `async def` — logging, tracing, metrics, anything of that shape):

- `PermissionEngine._rule_matches` calls the hook through `_execute_async_or_sync_func`;
- that helper decided whether to await with `inspect.iscoroutinefunction`, which reports `False` for the sync wrapper;
- the wrapper returns the coroutine, the helper returned it **un-awaited**;
- `if await self._rule_matches(...)` then evaluated a truthy coroutine object, so **any** rule for that tool matched **every** input.

In the report's repro an ALLOW rule for `git status` let `curl ... | sh` through as `allow`. Deny/ask rules for the tool matched every input as well. The only signal was a `RuntimeWarning: coroutine ... was never awaited`.

## Root cause

Deciding async-ness by *inspecting the callable* is not reliable: decorators are transparent to the wrapped function but opaque to `inspect.iscoroutinefunction`.

## Change

`_execute_async_or_sync_func` now decides from the **result**:

```python
result = func(*args, **kwargs)
if inspect.isawaitable(result):
    return await result
return result
```

This covers the decorated coroutine, `functools.partial`, plain sync returns and future wrapper shapes without guessing. The now-unused `_is_async_func` helper is removed, along with its `asyncio` / `functools` / `types` imports.

All three call sites go through this helper (`PermissionEngine._rule_matches`, `_generate_suggestions`, and the batch de-duplication in `Agent`), so they are all fixed at once. Sync `match_rule` overrides in third-party tools keep working unchanged.

## Verification

New test in `tests/permission_engine_test.py` (`DecoratedMatchRuleTest`): a tool whose `async def match_rule` is wrapped by a `functools.wraps` sync decorator, with an ALLOW rule for `git status`. Its `check_permissions` returns a non-safety ASK so rule matching actually runs.

- `git status` → `ALLOW` (the rule matches the command it names);
- `curl example.com | sh` → **not** `ALLOW`.

```
uv run python -m pytest tests/permission_engine_test.py -q
with the change:                     18 passed, 22 skipped, 156 subtests passed
with _common.py reverted:             1 failed, 17 passed
```

The failure without the change is exactly the reported fail-open:

```
AssertionError: <PermissionBehavior.ALLOW: 'allow'> == <PermissionBehavior.ALLOW: 'allow'>
```

i.e. the non-matching command was still allowed.

Related suites:

```
uv run python -m pytest tests/permission_engine_test.py tests/permission_mode_test.py -q
46 passed, 46 skipped, 156 subtests passed

uv run python -m pytest tests/agent_basic_test.py -q
18 passed
```

title: fix(agent): count rounds completed during HITL resumption toward max_iters
body:
## AgentScope Version

`2.0.12dev`

## Description

Rounds completed during HITL resumption were not counted toward `max_iters`. External execution results and rejected confirmations can finish a parked round inside `_handle_incoming_event`, before the reasoning–acting loop resumes. Repeatedly completing rounds through these paths leaves `cur_iter` unchanged, bypassing the iteration budget.

After handling an incoming event, count the round if no unfinished tool calls remain, using the same completion check as the loop. Partial resumptions remain uncounted until the last tool call finishes. Approved confirmations still complete and count inside the loop.

Fixes #3644

### Test coverage

Add five regression tests covering:

- External execution results enforcing the iteration budget.
- Rejected confirmations enforcing the iteration budget.
- Partial external results counting a round exactly once.
- Approved confirmations counting a round exactly once.
- Consecutive external resumptions exhausting a `max_iters=2` budget.

Three tests also verify that forced finalization uses `tool_choice.mode == "none"`.

### How to test

Use Python 3.11 with the development dependencies installed:

```bash
uv pip install -e ".[dev]"
pytest -q tests
pre-commit run --all-files
```

title: fix(tool): prevent CPython startup hangs in exec_shell on Windows
body:
Fixes #3643

On Windows, a CPython process launched by `LocalBackend.exec_shell()` can hang during interpreter startup if it inherits a named pipe as stdin from a host such as Electron. This leaves `exec_shell()` waiting for the child to exit.

`LocalBackend.exec_shell()` now passes `stdin=asyncio.subprocess.DEVNULL` when spawning a child. On all platforms, commands that previously read from the host's stdin now receive EOF. Commands that read from a file, an explicit shell pipe, or redirected input still get their input from that source.

## Verification

- Windows 11, CPython 3.12, Electron host (PR author): all nine subprocess probes completed with the fix, and the end-to-end turn completed.
- macOS: with data piped into the host, the child read EOF and the host could still read the original data. All 33 tests in `backend_local_test.py` passed.

v1 maintenance branch, 1.0.21.

## Description

Fixes #1426.

title: fix(app): fail wakeup dispatcher startup when subscription dies early
body:
## AgentScope Version

`2.0.12dev` (`main` at `4acacb9f`)

## Description

Fixes #3630.

If the wakeup subscription failed before calling `on_ready`, `WakeupDispatcher.__aenter__()` never returned. `_loop()` logged the error and exited, but startup only waited on `ready`, so app startup hung with nothing in the caller's hands.

Startup now waits on readiness and on the loop task together (`asyncio.wait(..., FIRST_COMPLETED)`):

- If `ready` is set first, startup continues exactly as before.
- If the loop ends first, `__aenter__` re-raises the subscription's error, or a `RuntimeError` if the subscription ended without one. It never reports a start that did not happen.
- On that failure, and when startup itself is cancelled, the loop task is cancelled, awaited and cleared before the exception propagates. `__aexit__` does not run when `__aenter__` raises, so this cleanup has to live in `__aenter__`.

`_loop()` now re-raises only when the error comes before `on_ready`. An error after the subscription went live is still logged and swallowed, as today. As the issue suggests, `ready` is not set from the exception handler.

In `_lifespan.py` the dispatcher is entered through the `AsyncExitStack`, so a failed subscription now fails app startup and unwinds the contexts entered before it.

### Tests

Four new tests in `TestWakeupDispatcherLifecycle` (`tests/service_wakeup_dispatcher_test.py`):

- `test_subscription_failure_before_ready_fails_startup`: the issue's `FailingBus` case. `__aenter__` raises the `ConnectionError`, `_task` is cleared, and no startup signal is published.
- `test_subscription_ending_before_ready_fails_startup`: a subscription that returns before `on_ready` raises `RuntimeError`.
- `test_cancelled_startup_cancels_loop`: cancelling `__aenter__` while the subscription is still connecting cancels the loop task and clears `_task`.
- `test_startup_returns_only_after_subscription_is_live`: a happy-path guard. `__aenter__` stays pending until `on_ready`, and the startup signal is published only after it.

The first three fail on `main` (the first two time out, the third leaves the loop task running). The fourth passes on both, since it pins down existing behaviour.

Run locally on Python 3.11, as in CI:

```
$ pytest tests/service_wakeup_dispatcher_test.py
51 passed, 10 subtests passed

$ coverage run -m pytest tests -v
3152 passed, 147 skipped, 1408 subtests passed

$ pre-commit run --all-files
all hooks Passed (mypy, black, flake8, pylint included)
```

The issue's own reproduction now prints `startup raised: ConnectionError('subscription failed before on_ready')` instead of timing out.

### Notes for reviewers

- Three open PRs also edit `_wakeup_dispatcher.py`: #2515 (backlog drain), #2682 (retry backoff) and #3100 (per-trigger dispatch errors). None of them touches the readiness wait. This diff is kept to `__aenter__` and the `except` in `_loop()` so it overlaps with them as little as possible. #2515 changes the line right after `await ready.wait()`, so whichever lands second has a small, mechanical conflict there.
- Cleanup on failure is limited to the loop task, which is all that exists before readiness. A failure in the startup `publish` after readiness still leaves the fallback task to `__aexit__`, as today. I kept that out of scope.
- An alternative is to call `__aexit__()` from the failure path. I avoided it because it also closes the chat input queue and releases recovery leadership through the bus, which has just failed.

title: fix(tool): report Write failures as error chunks
body:
Fixes #3637

## Summary

`Write.call` awaits `backend.write_file` without guarding it, so an I/O failure of the filesystem escapes the tool as a raw exception. The sibling file tools do not behave this way: `Read` wraps the whole read (`_read.py:509-613`) and `Edit` wraps both its read and its write (`_edit.py:343-408`, emitting `Error writing file: ...`). `Write` is the only builtin file tool that can raise out of `ToolBase.__call__` for a plain filesystem error.

## What breaks

Any destination the OS rejects propagates an `OSError` subclass out of the tool: a parent component that is a regular file, a directory used as the destination, or a path without write permission. Reproducer against `main` (`4acacb9`), with `PYTHONPATH=src`:

```python
import asyncio, os, tempfile
from agentscope.tool import Write, Edit, Read

async def main():
    root = tempfile.mkdtemp()
    blocker = os.path.join(root, "blocker.txt")
    with open(blocker, "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        f.write("not a directory\n")
    child = os.path.join(blocker, "report.csv")
    for name, tool, kwargs in (
        ("Write", Write(), {"file_path": child, "content": "a,b\n"}),
        ("Edit", Edit(), {"file_path": child, "old_string": "a", "new_string": "b"}),
        ("Read", Read(), {"file_path": child}),
    ):
        try:
            res = await tool(**kwargs)
        except Exception as e:
            print(f"{name}: RAISED {type(e).__name__}: {e}")
            continue
        print(f"{name}: STATE={res.state.value} TEXT={res.content[0].text!r}")

asyncio.run(main())
```

Observed on main:

```
Write: RAISED FileExistsError: [WinError 183] xxx: 'C:\\Users\\...\\blocker.txt'
Edit: STATE=error TEXT='Error: File not found: C:\\Users\\...\\blocker.txt\\report.csv'
Read: STATE=error TEXT='Error: File does not exist: C:\\Users\\...\\blocker.txt\\report.csv'
```

The exception finally lands in the generic `except Exception` of `Toolkit.call_tool` (`_toolkit.py:333`), which stringifies it into the tool result. So the model receives a bare OS message with no hint of which operation failed, and this failure takes a different path than every other failure the same call can return (`file_path must be an absolute path`, `File ... exists but has not been read yet`, ...), all of which are proper `ToolResultState.ERROR` chunks. Callers using the tool outside the agent loop get an exception instead of a ToolChunk at all.

## Change

Guard the write in `_write.py` exactly the way `Edit` already guards its own, returning a `ToolResultState.ERROR` chunk with `Error writing file: ...`. One file, +11/-4, plus the regression test.

## Verification

Python 3.13.14 / pytest on Windows 11, `PYTHONPATH=src` pointed at the checkout. No model, no credentials, no network.

Regression test `WriteToolTest.test_write_failure_returns_error_chunk`, added to the existing `tests/builtin_write_test.py`. It only creates a temp file and uses it as a parent component, so it fails deterministically for every user and platform.

Before the fix:

```
$ python -m pytest tests/builtin_write_test.py -q
tests\builtin_write_test.py:196:
src\agentscope\tool\_base.py:222: in __call__
    return await self.call(**kwargs)
src\agentscope\tool\_builtin\_write.py:299: in call
    await self._backend.write_file(
src\agentscope\tool\_builtin\_backend.py:864: in write_file
    os.makedirs(parent, exist_ok=True)
E   FileExistsError: [WinError 183] xxx: 'C:\\Users\\...\\blocker.txt'
FAILED tests/builtin_write_test.py::WriteToolTest::test_write_failure_returns_error_chunk
1 failed, 11 passed, 4 subtests passed in 3.03s
```

After the fix:

```
$ python -m pytest tests/builtin_write_test.py -q
12 passed, 4 subtests passed in 2.84s
```

The reproducer now prints, in line with `Edit`/`Read`:

```
Write: STATE=error TEXT="Error writing file: [WinError 183] xxx: 'C:\\Users\\...\\blocker.txt'"
```

Re-ran without regressions: `tests/builtin_write_test.py` and `builtin_edit_test.py` for the change itself, plus `builtin_read_test.py`, `builtin_glob_test.py`, `builtin_file_cache_test.py`, `builtin_file_cache_backend_test.py` and `toolkit_test.py` (121 passed in total for the set that can run here).

Linters, pinned to the `rev`s in `.pre-commit-config.yaml` (black 23.3.0, flake8 6.1.0, mypy 1.7.0, pylint 3.0.2), run only on the two files I touched:

```
$ python -m black --line-length=79 --check src/agentscope/tool/_builtin/_write.py tests/builtin_write_test.py
All done!  2 files would be left unchanged.
$ python -m flake8 --extend-ignore=E203 src/agentscope/tool/_builtin/_write.py tests/builtin_write_test.py
(empty, exit 0)
$ python -m mypy --disallow-untyped-defs --disallow-incomplete-defs --ignore-missing-imports --disable-error-code=var-annotated --disable-error-code=union-attr --disable-error-code=assignment --disable-error-code=attr-defined --disable-error-code=import-untyped --disable-error-code=truthy-function --disable-error-code=typeddict-item --follow-imports=skip --explicit-package-bases src/agentscope/tool/_builtin/_write.py tests/builtin_write_test.py
Success: no issues found in 2 source files
$ python -m pylint <pre-commit disables, max-branches=30, ...> src/agentscope/tool/_builtin/_write.py tests/builtin_write_test.py
Your code has been rated at 10.00/10
```

(The pylint command replicates the argument list from `.pre-commit-config.yaml` in full; the abbreviated version above is just the long flag list.)

## Duplicate search

I searched issues **and** PRs, open and closed, before changing anything. Nothing describes or fixes this.

- `Write OSError` -> only #3508 (LocalBackend truncates before writing) and #3442 / #3144 (blob store, workspace add_skill)
- `Write tool PermissionError` -> only #3511, the fix for #3508
- `IsADirectoryError` -> 0 hits
- `"Error writing file"` -> only #338, closed, unrelated
- Open PR list filtered on `tool` / `write file` / `builtin`: the open PRs that touch `_write.py` are #3214 (split lines at newlines only) and #3244 (shared diff helper); neither touches the `write_file` call site.

#3508 / #3511 are adjacent but a different defect: they are about a partial write being published, this is about the failure leaving the tool as an exception. The two fixes can coexist.

## What I did not run

- Verified only on Windows (Python 3.13.14). The failing condition used by the test is shared by POSIX (`os.makedirs` raises `FileExistsError` when a parent component is a regular file, for root too), but I did not execute it on Linux or macOS.
- `tests/builtin_grep_test.py` fails in my environment for an unrelated reason: no `rg` binary installed (`ripgrep error (code 127)`). It fails identically before my change.
- I did not run the parts of `pytest tests` that need Docker, model API keys, or network access, and I did not run the web UI / service stack.

## AgentScope Version

2.0.12dev (main @ `4acacb9`)

## Description

`CosyVoiceModel.push()` (realtime mode) silently drops the current text delta when `streaming_call` raises **after** the cold-start latch is set (`src/agentscope/tts/_dashscope/_cosyvoice_model.py:286-291`): the `except` branch returns `TTSResponse(content=None)` based on a recovery promise ("keep the cold-start buffer and flag intact so the next push retries it") that only holds during the cold-start phase. Once the latch is set the buffer is empty, so the failed delta exists only in `_accumulated_text` and is never sent — the synthesized speech silently misses words, with no error or log (#3620).

The surrounding code consistently chooses otherwise: the `not self._connected` guard right above raises, and `_synthesize_realtime` retries and eventually raises. #3535 built the cold-start failure handling this comment refers to — the post-cold-start path is its remaining gap.

**Changes** — the `except` branch now distinguishes the two phases:

- cold-start flush failure (`not self._cold_start_done`): unchanged — keep the buffer and flag intact so the next push retries the whole buffered text (#3535 behavior preserved);
- post-cold-start failure: **raise**, consistent with the `_connected` guard above — the caller still holds the text and can retry, instead of the delta vanishing from the synthesized speech.

title: fix(memory): extend the frontmatter read to the closing fence when the byte cap cuts it off
body:
## AgentScope Version

2.0.12dev (main @ `4acacb9`)

## Description

The agentic-memory indexer reads only a byte-capped prefix of each memory file before parsing frontmatter (`retrieval_max_tokens_per_frontmatter` defaults to 256 tokens = 1024 bytes). The parsing regex requires a closing fence, so when the frontmatter block itself outgrows the cap the fence sits outside the prefix, the regex cannot match, and the file's `description` / `type` metadata are **all silently dropped** from the memory index (#3616 has the repro). #3345 already fixed the sibling case where only the trailing newline falls outside the prefix.

**Changes** — extract the prefix computation into `_frontmatter_snippet` and extend the read window to the closing fence when one exists beyond the cap:

```python
closing = raw.find(b"\n---", 1)
if closing != -1:
    newline = raw.find(b"\n", closing + 1)
    fence_end = len(raw) if newline == -1 else newline + 1
    snippet_end = max(snippet_end, min(len(raw), fence_end))
```

The fence sits near the top of the file by definition, so the extension is bounded; `raw` is already fully in memory (`read_file`), so nothing extra is read. Behavior matrix:

| file | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| frontmatter longer than the cap, fence beyond it | all metadata lost | **fully recovered** |
| closing fence at end of file, no trailing newline | kept (#3345) | kept |
| no closing fence (malformed) | capped prefix, `{}` | unchanged |
| frontmatter inside the cap | unchanged | unchanged |

**How to test**

Three regression cases added to the existing `FrontmatterParseTest` in `tests/middleware_filesystem_memory_test.py`: the over-cap file now yields `description` + `type` through the extended window; the unclosed and within-cap shapes are pinned to their current behavior.

```bash
python -m pytest tests/middleware_filesystem_memory_test.py
```

title: fix(ollama): declare ResponseError as fallback-eligible so the structured-output ladder can switch strategies
body:
## AgentScope Version

2.0.12dev (main @ `4acacb9`)

## Description

`OllamaChatModel` is the only mainline provider that does not override `_get_structured_output_fallback_exceptions` (base returns `()`). In the structured-output strategy ladder (`model/_base.py:565-594`), an exception that is neither retryable nor fallback-eligible raises immediately — so for Ollama, any server-side rejection (`ollama.ResponseError`, which the SDK uses for every non-transport failure including 4xx) kills the whole ladder on the first attempt, and the `auto` / `no_think` / `none` strategies are never tried.

**Changes** — declare the fallback exception, verbatim provider style:

```python
@classmethod
def _get_structured_output_fallback_exceptions(cls) -> tuple[Type[Exception], ...]:
    from ollama import ResponseError

    # ResponseError wraps every server-side rejection (including 4xx
    # like "model not found" or a tools/structured-output refusal) into
    # a single type, so the structured-output ladder must fall through
    # on it instead of aborting. Transport-level failures stay
    # retryable via the httpx set above.
    return (ResponseError,)
```

The retryable set (three httpx transport errors) stays untouched — transport failures keep retrying, protocol-level rejections now switch strategies. Same series as #3583/#3588 (Ollama thinking toggle) and #3612/#3613 (Gemini 4xx fall-through).

**How to test**

Regression cases added to the existing `tests/model_ollama_test.py`:

- `test_fallback_exceptions_declare_response_error` — fails on `main` (`() != (ResponseError,)`);
- `test_response_error_walks_the_ladder` — records every `_call_api` attempt while the ladder degrades: on `main` a mocked `ResponseError` dies after `1` attempt; with this fix all four strategies are tried (`4 attempts`).

title: fix(gemini): let 4xx fall through the structured-output ladder and gate the no_think strategy by model
body:
## AgentScope Version

2.0.12dev (main @ `2350af9`)

## Description

`GeminiChatModel` is the only mainline provider without a `_get_structured_output_fallback_exceptions` override, and its `_get_retryable_exceptions` returns the wide `(google.genai.errors.APIError,)` (`model/_gemini/_model.py:250-258`) — the parent of both `ClientError` (4xx) and `ServerError` (5xx). In the structured-output ladder, the retryable check runs before the fallback check, and retry-exhaustion raises unconditionally (`model/_base.py:582`). So any 4xx aborts the whole ladder — the `auto` / `no_think` / `none` strategies are never tried. Every other provider declares a narrow retryable set whose members never intersect its fallback tuple, so 4xx falls through for them.

**Changes**

1. `model/_base.py` (give-up branch): when a retryable exception exhausts its retries but is *also* fallback-eligible, walk the ladder instead of raising. Providers whose retryable and fallback sets are disjoint (all but Gemini today) are unaffected — the new branch is unreachable for them. A purely transient error that is not fallback-eligible still raises as before.
2. `model/_gemini/_model.py`: declare `_get_structured_output_fallback_exceptions` → `(errors.ClientError,)` so 4xx switches strategies (5xx stay retryable).
3. `model/_gemini/_model.py`: implement `_get_disable_thinking_kwargs`, the same gap #3583/#3588 fixed for Ollama, gated by model — 2.5 Flash / Flash-Lite accept `thinking_budget: 0`, but the pro models reject it with 400 and Gemini 3 deprecates `thinking_budget`, so those return `{}` and keep the server default.

Complementary to #3523 (tri-state `thinking_enable`): that fix stopped out-of-the-box budget-0 failures for pro models; this adds the structured-output no_think step for the models that support it.

**Open question for maintainers**: with the give-up branch consulting the fallback tuple, a 429 (also a `ClientError`) now falls to the next strategy after its retries instead of aborting — bounded extra calls to a rate-limited endpoint. If that is undesirable, the alternative is gating the no_think kwargs more narrowly and leaving the base branch untouched, at the cost of keeping the abort for schema-type 4xx.

## How to test

Regression cases added to the existing test files:

- `tests/model_base_test.py::StructuredOutputRetryableFallbackTest` — an exception that is both retryable and fallback-eligible walks the ladder after exhausting retries (fails on `main`: the ladder aborts);

## AgentScope Version

2.0.12dev

## Description

Fixes #3609

### Problem

When creating a scheduled task in the Web UI, the selected start date and time were not submitted to the backend. The backend therefore used the creation time as the start boundary, allowing tasks to execute early. This affects all four frequencies: Daily, Weekly, Monthly, and Once.

### Changes

- Add an optional `started_at` field to frontend and backend creation requests.

- Require a UTC offset for non-null start times and persist them in the existing field. Omitted or `null` values retain the timezone-aware creation-time default.
- Reuse existing scheduler and boundary validation without adding dependencies or database migrations.
- Reject nonexistent local start times and resolve ambiguous local start times to the earlier UTC instant.

Existing Cron rules remain unchanged for each frequency. Annual recurrence for Once is outside the scope of this fix.

title: fix(schedule): serialize reconciliation so stale reads cannot restore jobs
body:
## PR Title Format

`fix(schedule): serialize reconciliation so stale reads cannot restore jobs`

## AgentScope Version

`2.0.12dev` (main at `2350af90`)

## Description

**Background.** `SchedulerManager.reconcile()` is the only writer of the local
APScheduler job set, and two independent callers drive it: the periodic
`_periodic()` loop and the lifecycle `_listen()` subscription. Nothing ordered
their storage reads, so two reconciles could overlap:

```text
A: list_all_schedules() -> captures version-1 (enabled)
B: list_all_schedules() -> captures version-2 (disabled)
B: apply                 -> removes the job
A: apply                 -> re-adds the job from version-1
```

The same interleaving restores an edited schedule's previous cron and
`updated_at`. The result is a job that storage says is deleted or disabled
being registered again, and an old configuration being used for the next fire.

**Change.** `SchedulerManager` now owns an `asyncio.Lock`; `reconcile()` holds
it across the storage read and the resulting job updates, and the previous body
moved to `_reconcile_locked()`. Serialising the read with the apply is what
makes the ordering complete: the last reconcile to finish is always the one
that read the newest snapshot. Writes still use `notify_changed()` and the
periodic fallback, so a dropped notification heals as before.

**Validation.**

* Two deterministic regression tests pause the first storage read, mutate
  storage (disable or edit), and start a second reconcile while the first one
  is still holding its snapshot. On unmodified `main` both tests fail:
  the disabled job is re-added and the edited job reverts to version 1.
* With the fix, the second read waits for the first reconcile, then applies the
  new state; both tests pass.
* `tests/service_scheduler_test.py`: 19 passed.
* `tests/schedule_router_test.py` + `tests/service_toolkit_test.py`: 21 passed,
  5 subtests passed.
* `black --line-length=79` (no new formatting issues), `flake8
  --extend-ignore=E203`, `pylint` (10.00/10) and `mypy` (pre-commit flags) are
  clean.

Fixes #3344.

title: feat(app): make the tool offload timeout configurable via create_app
body:
## AgentScope Version

```
2.0.12.dev0 (main @ 9f59a369)
```

## Description

**Problem.** `ChatService` hardwires `ToolOffloadMiddleware(...)` with its default
`timeout_secs=10.0`, and neither `create_app` nor `ChatService` exposes that knob. In a
request/response deployment (one AG-UI run per HTTP request) a tool that needs 10–30 s gets
offloaded at 10 s, and the continuation turn lands after the stream has closed — the client never
sees the result and it races the user's next message. The current workaround (a custom agent class
that filters the middleware out) depends on how `ChatService` builds its middleware list
internally.

**Changes.**

- `create_app(..., tool_offload_timeout_secs: float | None = 10.0)` — stored on `app.state` and
  forwarded to `ChatService`.
- `ChatService(..., tool_offload_timeout_secs: float | None = 10.0)` — `None` means the middleware
  is not attached at all (tools keep their own timeouts); a number is passed through as
  `timeout_secs`.
- The default is unchanged: `10.0`.

**How to test.**

```
python -c "import inspect; from agentscope.app import create_app; print(inspect.signature(create_app).parameters['tool_offload_timeout_secs'].default)"
# -> 10.0
```

`ruff check src/agentscope/app/` passes. The app integration tests
(`app_lifespan_dedicated_test.py`) fail on this machine for an unrelated reason — the pinned
`fakeredis` does not implement the `eval` command the session store uses — so the behavioural

title: fix(scheduler): honor standard cron day alternatives
body:
Fixes #3601.

## AgentScope Version

`2.0.12dev`; based on upstream main `3ca8dc309572851a5b884aa36d51f9a164b30cd3`.

## Description

The API documents standard five-field cron, but one APScheduler `CronTrigger` intersects the two restricted day fields. `0 9 1 * 1`, queried after 2026-10-02, consequently skips all October/November runs and returns 2027-02-01 instead of 2026-10-05.

Use APScheduler's existing `OrTrigger` only when both original day fields are restricted (neither contains `*`). The alternatives share all minute/hour/month fields, timezone, and start/end bounds. A coincident date is one fire. Existing wildcard and stepped-wildcard behavior stays conjunctive. No dependency, public schedule-input API, or persisted-expression migration is added.

The change includes behavior-focused tests for:

- The complete monthly-plus-weekly date sequence, not the trigger's internal representation.
- Coincident day matches producing one run.
- Timezone and start/end bounds on both alternatives.
- Wildcard and stepped-wildcard day fields retaining their behavior.
- An impossible month day still allowing matching weekdays.
- Invalid weekday expressions still being rejected.

Existing weekday normalization coverage now checks actual fire dates rather than APScheduler's incidental internal `fields` layout. Upstream's newer HTTP schedule-end-time tests are retained.

## Compatibility / Rollout

This intentionally corrects the advertised standard-cron behavior. Existing stored expressions are not rewritten; the corrected semantics take effect when jobs are registered again, including scheduler restart. Deployments that relied on the old AND behavior for two restricted day fields should review those schedules. The local changelog and validation docstring explain the change.

**Draft status:** implementation and local verification are complete. The draft requests maintainer confirmation of this behavior correction and rollout, rather than assuming policy approval. #2770 corrected weekday numbering and explicitly left this combination policy unchanged.

title: fix(middleware): retire the budget hint at a new reply boundary
body:
## AgentScope Version

```
2.0.12.dev0 (main @ 9f59a369)
```

## Description

**Problem.** `ReplyBudgetControlMiddleware` resets its per-reply counter on `ReplyStartEvent`, but
the `HintBlock` it injected after the budget was exhausted stays in `agent.state.context`. The next
reply therefore starts with a fresh budget and no forced `tool_choice`, yet its model input still
carries "you MUST wrap up immediately ... without invoking any tools" from the previous reply.

**Changes.**

- `src/agentscope/middleware/_budget.py`
  - The wrap-up hints are now tagged with `source='{"label": "System", "sublabel": "Reply Budget Exhausted"}''`, mirroring the label the max-iteration hint already uses.
  - `_retire_budget_hints()` removes only blocks carrying that tag when a new reply starts. Hints
    from other middleware, and every message that still has real content, are untouched; a message
    that held nothing but the hint is dropped with it.
  - The cleanup runs inside the `ReplyStartEvent` branch, so it fires on a genuinely new reply and
    never while the same reply is still running (HITL continuation keeps its budget semantics).

**How to test.**

```bash
cd tests && pytest middleware_budget_test.py -q
```

`test_new_reply_does_not_inherit_the_previous_budget_hint` drives two replies with
`token_budget=300`: the first spends 300 tokens on a tool call, so its second step runs under the
hint; the second reply starts fresh. It asserts the hint is present after reply 1 and gone after
reply 2.

title: fix(embedding): keep an unknown token count unknown when merging batches
body:
## What this fixes

Merging batched embedding responses loses the "unknown" state of the token count.

`EmbeddingModelBase._merge_responses` initialised the aggregate to `0` and only added a batch's count when it was truthy:

```python
total_tokens = 0
...
if resp.usage:
    total_time = max(total_time, resp.usage.time)
    if resp.usage.tokens:
        total_tokens += resp.usage.tokens
```

So for an OpenAI-compatible endpoint that omits `usage` (or reports `tokens=None`):

| input | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| 1 text (single batch) | `tokens=None` ✅ | `tokens=None` ✅ |
| 2049 texts (2 batches) | `tokens=0` ❌ | `tokens=None` ✅ |
| 2 batches, only one reported | `tokens=7` (partial sum) ❌ | `tokens=None` ✅ |
| 2 batches, both report `0` | `tokens=0` ✅ | `tokens=0` ✅ |

`EmbeddingUsage.tokens` is documented as the number of tokens used *if available*, so an unknown count should stay unknown after merging instead of turning into a zero or a partial sum that depends on how many input texts happened to land in one batch.

## Change

`total_tokens` starts at `0` and becomes `None` as soon as any batch cannot report a count (missing `usage` object, or `tokens is None`); once unknown it stays unknown for the rest of the merge. Genuine zeroes and reported counts sum exactly as before. `usage.time` still takes the maximum over the batches that did report usage.

## Tests

`tests/embedding_base_test.py` gains four cases:

- unknown count in a later batch → `None`
- unknown count in an earlier batch → `None` (order-independent)
- a batch with no `usage` object at all → `None`
- a genuine `0` plus a reported `3` → `3` (zero is a value, not "unknown")

The three "stays unknown" cases fail on `main` and pass with this change; the existing five tests are unchanged and still pass:

```
$ PYTHONPATH=src python -m pytest tests/embedding_base_test.py -q
9 passed
```

Fixes #3379.

## Description

`ChatModelBase.generate_structured_output` only includes the `no_think` strategy in its fallback ladder when the provider overrides `_get_disable_thinking_kwargs` (`src/agentscope/model/_base.py:509-524`). Five providers implement it, but `OllamaChatModel` does not — so for Ollama reasoning models (qwen3, deepseek-r1, ...) whose thinking output crowds out the structured payload, the ladder is only forced → auto → none and never attempts the `think=False` request that Ollama fully supports (the parameter path already maps `thinking_enable` to the top-level `think` option at `model/_ollama/_model.py:178-179`).

**Changes** — implement the override, verbatim provider style:

```python
def _get_disable_thinking_kwargs(self) -> dict:
    """Ollama uses a top-level ``think`` option."""
    return {"think": False}
```

Complementary to #3510 (Ollama `think` tri-state): that fix made the parameter tri-state; this makes the structured-output fallback actually use it. One interaction, documented correctly: `_call_api` writes `kwargs["think"] = parameters.thinking_enable` (`model/_ollama/_model.py:178-179`) **before** `kwargs.update(generate_kwargs)` (`:181`), so the `no_think` attempt's `think=False` overrides an explicit `thinking_enable=True` for that attempt — unlike the DashScope `setdefault` semantics; happy to align if maintainers prefer.

## How to test

Regression cases added to the existing `tests/model_ollama_test.py`:

- `test_disable_thinking_kwargs_is_think_false` — fails on `main` (`{} != {'think': False}`).
- `test_fallback_ladder_sends_think_false_and_parses` — mocks `client.chat` and asserts the ladder sends `think=False` on the third (no_think) attempt and that the returned tool arguments are parsed and validated. On `main` the same test fails with `[True, True, True] != [True, True, False]`.

```bash
python -m pytest tests/model_ollama_test.py
# 15 passed.
```

## Real environment reproduction

Reproduced with a real Ollama server (`0.40.3`, Windows, CPU), Python client `ollama 0.6.2`, and `qwen3:0.6b` (Q4_K_M; 751.63M parameters; default thinking `true`). Request: extract `{name: string, age: integer}` from "Alice is 30 years old and lives in Berlin." through the `generate_structured_output` tool; `temperature=0` (required for a deterministic repro — with the model's default sampling, one base-revision run succeeded on the second attempt).

Raw `/api/chat` with tools (3 runs each, identical):

| request | thinking | content | tool_calls |
|---|---|---|---|
| `think=true` | 465 chars | `""` | none (`done_reason=stop`, 138 eval tokens) |
| `think=false` | 0 | `""` | `{"name": "Alice", "age": 30}` (29 eval tokens) |

Through `generate_structured_output` (`thinking_enable=True, temperature=0`):

| revision | SDK `think` per attempt | tool calls | result |
|---|---|---|---|
| base `ea903c9` | `true, true, true` | `0, 0, 0` | `StructuredOutputError` |
| this PR | `true, true, false` | `0, 0, 1` | `{'name': 'Alice', 'age': 30}` |

The default `thinking_enable=None` configuration behaves the same (base fails, this PR succeeds), because `qwen3:0.6b` enables thinking by default. On Ollama the first three strategies are byte-identical (`tool_choice` is ignored and the `none` strategy still sends the tool schema), so the `no_think` attempt is the only request that differs.

title: fix(pipeline): clear the leader's parked TeamAssign when a member's model fails
body:
## Problem

Fixes #3577.

`TeamPipeline.reply_stream` only clears the leader's parked `TeamAssign` inside
`except asyncio.CancelledError`:

```python
try:
    async for evt in self._reply(inputs):
        yield evt
except asyncio.CancelledError:
    if self.leader.state.has_awaiting_tool_calls(self.leader.name):
        async for evt in self.reply_stream(UserInterruptEvent(...)):
            yield evt
    ...
```

When a member's model raises an ordinary exception (a transient transport
failure, for example), `_reply` propagates it and the leader stays parked on its
`TeamAssign`. Nothing else clears that call, so the next ordinary turn fails in
`has_awaiting_tool_calls`:

```
ValueError: Agent is waiting for 0 tool calls and external execution results
for 1 tool calls, but received no event.
```

## Fix

Run the same cleanup the interrupt path already uses, then re-raise:

```python
except Exception:
    if self.leader.state.has_awaiting_tool_calls(self.leader.name):
        async for evt in self.reply_stream(
            UserInterruptEvent(reply_id=self.leader.state.reply_id),
        ):
            yield evt
    raise
```

`GeneratorExit` is deliberately not covered — a consumer closing the stream is
not a member failure — which is why this is `except Exception` rather than
`except BaseException`.

## Test

`test_member_model_failure_clears_parked_assignment` uses a `_FailsOnceModel`
(built on the existing `MockModel`) so the member fails once and then recovers.
It asserts that:

1. the first turn raises the member's `RuntimeError`,
2. the leader no longer has awaiting tool calls afterwards, and
3. the next ordinary `UserMsg` completes with a `REPLY_END` from the leader.

No live provider is needed.

body:
## AgentScope Version

2.0.12dev (based on main at 2f8c0299)

## Description

DashScope text embedding responses carry text_index, and multimodal responses carry index; both fields identify the input position. The adapter currently discards them and returns vectors in response-array order. If indexed entries arrive out of order, the vectors are assigned to the wrong inputs. In text mode, FileEmbeddingCache then persists that incorrect ordering.

This change restores input order for both SDK response paths when every entry has its documented index. Responses without indices retain their existing positional behavior. There is no public API change.

The touched file had a pre-existing mypy error: its parameter annotation referred to DashScopeEmbeddingModel.Parameters, which mypy cannot resolve. The annotation now names the inherited EmbeddingModelBase.Parameters so the changed file passes the repository's required hook.

- Two offline regression tests feed reversed indexed responses through the public model wrapper. Both failed against main with vectors in the wrong order; both pass after the fix. The text test also verifies that the corrected order is cached.
- Relevant embedding suites: 35 passed, 6 subtests passed.
- All pre-commit hooks for the changed files passed, including mypy, Black, Flake8, and Pylint; git diff --check passed.

title: fix(tracing): preserve zero top_p in _get_llm_request_attributes (#3515)
body:
## PR Title Format

fix(tracing): preserve zero top_p in _get_llm_request_attributes

## AgentScope Version

2.0.12dev

## Description

Fixes #3515.

### Background & Problem
In `agentscope.middleware._tracing._extractor._get_llm_request_attributes`, generation parameters are extracted from model call keyword arguments to populate OpenTelemetry GenAI span attributes:
```python
SpanAttributes.GEN_AI_REQUEST_TOP_P: kwargs.get("p") or kwargs.get("top_p"),
```
Because `0` and `0.0` are falsy in Python:
1. When greedy decoding is used with `p=0` (or `p=0.0`) and `top_p` is not set, `0 or None` evaluates to `None`. The resulting dictionary comprehension `if v is not None` filters it out, completely dropping `gen_ai.request.top_p` when deterministic greedy sampling is explicitly requested.
2. When `p=0` is provided to override a fallback `top_p=0.8`, `0 or 0.8` evaluates to `0.8`, ignoring the caller's explicit greedy setting.

### Changes Made
- Changed `kwargs.get("p") or kwargs.get("top_p")` to:
  ```python
  kwargs.get("p") if kwargs.get("p") is not None else kwargs.get("top_p")
  ```
  This preserves `0` and `0.0` when provided under either key, prioritizing `p` if specified, and falling back to `top_p` only when `p` is `None`.
- Added unit tests in `tests/tracing_test.py` (`TracingExtractorTest.test_llm_request_attributes_preserves_zero_top_p`) covering:
  - `top_p=0` preservation
  - `p=0` preservation
  - `p=0` taking precedence over `top_p=0.8`
  - `p=0.0` float preservation
  - fallback to `top_p` when `p` is `None`
  - omission of `gen_ai.request.top_p` when neither parameter is supplied
- Verified that all new code conforms to `black --line-length=79` and `flake8` checks without warnings.

body:
## AgentScope Version

`2.0.12dev` (based on upstream `main` at `07fda8fa`)

## Description

Fixes #3555.

Deleting a knowledge base previously removed every uploaded source blob before asking the knowledge-base manager to delete the vector collection and storage records. A vector-store error left the knowledge base and document records in place while the source files had already been destroyed. The user then saw a 500 on deletion and a 404 when trying to download the still-listed document.

It injects a vector-store failure, verifies that the document remains listed and downloadable, retries deletion, and verifies the blob is then gone. title: fix(rag): normalize MongoDB euclidean scores
body:
## Summary
- negate MongoDB Atlas vector-search distances when the collection uses `euclidean`
- preserve the shared `VectorSearchResult.score` higher-is-better contract used by knowledge-base merging and score thresholds
- add a regression test for raw MongoDB euclidean distances

## Root cause
MongoDB returns a lower-is-better distance for `euclidean` vector search, but `MongoDBStore.search()` returned it unchanged. This made more distant chunks receive higher scores and caused incorrect merged ordering and threshold filtering. Qdrant and Milvus already negate distance metrics.

## Reproduction
1. Construct `MongoDBStore(distance="euclidean")`.
2. Return a document with MongoDB `vectorSearchScore = 2.5`.
3. Call `search()`; before this fix the result score is `2.5` instead of `-2.5`.

## Tests

- Confirmed the new regression test fails with only the source change reverted and passes after restoring it.

title: fix(permission): await async match_rule hooks wrapped by sync decorators
body:
## AgentScope Version

2.0.12dev (main)

## Description

Fixes #3551

**Background.** `_execute_async_or_sync_func` decided whether to `await` by checking `inspect.iscoroutinefunction` before calling the function. If a tool's `async def match_rule` is wrapped by an ordinary sync decorator (anything built with `functools.wraps` that returns `fn(*args, **kwargs)`), that check returns `False`, so the helper returned the coroutine object without awaiting it. A coroutine object is truthy, so an allow rule for that tool matched every input and the permission check failed open. Deny and ask rules matched every input too.

**Changes**
- `_execute_async_or_sync_func` now calls the function and awaits the result when `inspect.isawaitable(result)` is true. Plain sync overrides still return their value unchanged. This also covers objects with an `async def __call__` and `functools.partial` of async functions. A partial of a bare async function already worked on 3.12, but not on 3.11.
- `PermissionEngine._rule_matches` raises a `TypeError` when `match_rule` doesn't return a `bool`, so a stray truthy value can't make the check fail open again.
- Removed `_is_async_func`. It was only used by this helper.

All three callers go through this helper: `PermissionEngine._rule_matches`, `PermissionEngine._generate_suggestions`, and the agent's batch de-duplication.

**Tests**
- Added regression tests for the helper: decorated async functions, async callables, partials, and sync overrides.
- Added `PermissionEngine` tests with a decorated async `match_rule`, covering allow, deny and ask rules plus `generate_suggestions` and a non-bool return value.
- Before the fix, 10 of the 22 new tests fail. After the fix, all 22 pass.
- `tests/permission_engine_test.py`, `tests/permission_mode_test.py`, `tests/builtin_bash_test.py` and `tests/common_async_exec_test.py` all pass: 137 passed, 44 subtests passed.

## AgentScope Version

2.0.12dev (main at `e763b351`)

## Description

Fixes #3549.

**Root cause**: `BubblewrapBackend._bwrap_argv()` ends every sandboxed command with `--clearenv` + `--setenv` pairs (`--clearenv` needs bwrap >= 0.5.0; Ubuntu 20.04 LTS ships 0.4.0), but the availability gate `BWRAP_SMOKE_PROBE_ARGV` never exercised that option. Unsupported builds now fail the probe and surface the existing clear startup error instead of failing later on every operation. Silently dropping `--clearenv` on old builds was not considered — it would let host environment variables leak into the sandbox.

title: feat(formatter): make OpenAI chat message names match the API pattern
body:
## AgentScope Version

2.0.12dev (main @ e763b351)

## Description

**Problem.** `OpenAIChatFormatter` copies `Msg.name` verbatim into the `name` field of every user/assistant message. The Chat Completions API only accepts names matching `^[^\s<|\\/>]+$`, and rejects anything else with:

```
400 Invalid 'messages[1].name': string does not match pattern.
Expected a string that matches the pattern '^[^\s<|\\/>]+$'.
```

Agent and user names are free text. For example, `AgentData.name` in the app is a plain string set in the web UI, and the chat service builds the agent with `name=agent_record.data.name`. An agent called "Research Assistant" writes its replies as `AssistantMsg(name="Research Assistant", ...)`. Once that reply is part of the context, every later request to an OpenAI chat model fails with a 400. `OpenAIMultiAgentFormatter` has the same problem, because it formats tool sequences through `OpenAIChatFormatter`.

Repro on main:

```python
import asyncio
from agentscope.formatter import OpenAIChatFormatter
from agentscope.message import UserMsg, AssistantMsg

msgs = [UserMsg("John Doe", "Hi"), AssistantMsg("Research Assistant", "Hello")]
print([m.get("name") for m in asyncio.run(OpenAIChatFormatter().format(msgs))])
# main:  ['John Doe', 'Research Assistant']   -> rejected by the API
# fixed: ['John_Doe', 'Research_Assistant']
```

**Fix.** Add a small helper, `_format_message_name`, in `_openai_formatter.py` and use it at the three places that emit `msg.name`. It replaces each run of whitespace or `<|\/>` with `_`, and leaves the field out when the name is empty, since the API rejects an empty name too. Valid names pass through unchanged, including non-ASCII ones such as `小明`, so existing outputs (`"user"`, `"assistant"`, `"system-reminder"`, ...) stay the same. Tool message names (`block.name`) are function names that are already constrained and are left alone.

**Tests.** Added `test_chat_formatter_sanitizes_message_name` to `tests/formatter_openai_chat_test.py`. It covers:
- a user name with a space,
- an assistant name split by a mid-message tool result (both flush paths),
- all forbidden characters,
- an empty name,
- the multi-agent tool-sequence path.

The test fails on main (`'John Doe'` vs `'John_Doe'`) and passes with the fix.

Commands run (Python 3.12, `uv pip install -e ".[dev]"`):
- `pytest tests/formatter_openai_chat_test.py`: 17 passed (16 passed, 1 failed before the fix)
- `pytest tests/formatter_*_test.py tests/model_openai_chat_test.py tests/service_model_test.py tests/middleware_model_router_test.py tests/tracing_test.py tests/service_agent_interrupt_test.py -n 4`: 222 passed
- `pytest tests -n 4`: 2925 passed, 147 skipped
- `pre-commit run --files <changed files>`: all hooks passed (mypy, black, flake8, pylint, ...)

Not in this PR: `MoonshotChatFormatter` also forwards `msg.name`. I have not verified whether Moonshot enforces the same pattern, so it is unchanged here.

Fixes #3546

title: fix(schedule): respect selected end dates when creating schedules
body:
## AgentScope Version

`2.0.12dev`

## Description

Fixes #3545.

### Background & Problem

When creating a recurring task on the Web UI's **Schedule** page, the selected **End Date** is neither submitted nor saved. The backend record's `ended_at` remains `null`, allowing the task to continue running after the selected end date.

The problem involves three points:

1. The frontend stores the selected end date in `form.endDate` but does not include it in the creation request.
2. The backend's `CreateScheduleRequest` has no `ended_at` field.
3. `ended_at` is not set when constructing `ScheduleData`.

### Solution

- Add an optional `ended_at` field to the frontend and backend creation requests, and persist it in `ScheduleData`.
- Convert the selected end date to the final instant of that day (`23:59:59.999`) in the task's configured timezone, then submit it as a UTC ISO timestamp.
- Require an explicit UTC offset on `ended_at`: a naive timestamp is rejected with `422` instead of being interpreted in the schedule's timezone. The trigger could interpret it, but the persisted record would keep no zone information, so clients would read it back in their own timezone.
- Preserve the existing unbounded behavior when no end date is selected.
- Omit any end date remaining in the form when switching to a one-time task.
- Reuse the existing scheduler's boundary validation and execution limits without introducing new runtime dependencies.

For example, with timezone `Asia/Shanghai` and an end date of October 31, 2026, valid occurrences on that day are allowed, while occurrences on November 1 or later are excluded.

### How to Test

Automated regression tests cover:

- Persisting the end time through the HTTP creation endpoint and returning it in subsequent queries.
- Preserving unbounded behavior when the end time is omitted or explicitly set to `null`.
- Date conversion across different browser and task timezones, daylight-saving transitions, fractional UTC offsets, and year boundaries.
- Rejecting malformed end times, naive end times without a UTC offset, and end times earlier than the start time.
- Allowing valid occurrences on the final day and scheduling no occurrences after the end boundary.

Completed checks:

- Full Python test suite: 2,947 passed, 127 skipped.
- Frontend regression tests: 5 passed.
- `pre-commit run --all-files` passed.
- Frontend formatting checks, lint, and build passed.

Manual verification steps:

1. Create a Daily task on the Schedule page, specifying a timezone and End Date.
2. Open the task details after creation and confirm that the end time is saved.
3. Check the calendar and confirm that valid occurrences appear on the end date, with none on subsequent dates.
4. Create another task without an End Date and confirm that it remains unbounded.

### Documentation

This restores the intended behavior of the existing End Date field and adds no new user-facing configuration. I have not opened a documentation PR; I can add a note in [agentscope-ai/docs](https://github.com/agentscope-ai/docs) if the end-date semantics should be documented there.

title: fix(tts): use first Gemini audio candidate
body:
## AgentScope Version

`2.0.12dev` (based on upstream `main` at `c74c56cc`).

## Description

A Gemini `generate_content` response can contain multiple `candidates`, which are alternative outputs. `GeminiTTSModel` currently walks every candidate in both its batch and streaming parsers, treating alternative recordings as consecutive PCM segments. This can concatenate distinct spoken renditions into one WAV or interleave them in a stream. The Gemini chat model already selects `candidates[0]` instead.

This PR selects the first candidate in both TTS parsers while preserving all audio parts within that candidate. It does not change the public API or the single-candidate path.

### Reproduction

With two response candidates carrying `AAAA` and `BBBB` PCM, the batch parser previously returned a WAV containing `AAAABBBB`; the expected single recording contains `AAAA`.

With two streaming chunks whose candidate pairs contain `(AAAA, BBBB)` and `(CCCC, DDDD)`, the old parser emitted four audio chunks. The fixed parser emits two chunks containing the selected candidate's `AAAACCCC` audio.

The new regression tests failed against unmodified `main` with exactly those mismatches, then passed after the fix.

title: fix(tts): keep CosyVoice cold-start buffer when the send fails
body:
## Why

`DashScopeCosyVoiceTTSModel.push` empties the cold-start buffer **before** the send:

```python
text_to_send = self._cold_start_buffer
self._cold_start_buffer = ""          # cleared BEFORE the call
self._cold_start_done = True

try:
    self._synthesizer.streaming_call(text_to_send)
except Exception:
    return TTSResponse(content=None)   # text_to_send is gone
```

When `streaming_call` raises (WebSocket mid-teardown is the realistic case), the `except` swallows the failure without restoring either — the buffered text is lost and cold start is latched done, so the audio for that chunk is silently dropped on a `realtime=True, cold_start_length=None` first push.

The realtime sibling does it in the safe order — `_realtime_model.py` calls `append_text(self._cold_start_buffer)` first and only clears the buffer and sets the flag on success, so a failed send leaves the text queued for `synthesize()` to flush (covered there by `test_synthesize_flushes_cold_start_buffer`).

Partial recovery exists today (`_accumulated_text` still holds the text, so `_synthesize_realtime` can replay it on a retry path) — but that costs a reconnect plus a `retry_delay`, and only if `streaming_complete()` happens to raise. If the synthesizer is merely broken rather than raising, the text is gone.

Repro:

```python
async with DashScopeCosyVoiceTTSModel(..., realtime=True, cold_start_length=10) as model:
    synthesizer.streaming_call = Mock(side_effect=RuntimeError("socket gone"))
    res = await model.push("Hi there friend!")
    # before: res.content is None, model._cold_start_buffer == "",
    #         model._cold_start_done == True  -> text lost
    # after:  buffer intact, flag not latched; next push retries the text
```

## What

- Move the buffer clear and the `_cold_start_done` latch to **after** a successful `streaming_call`, mirroring the realtime model's order. The happy-path behavior is unchanged; a failed send now leaves the buffered text queued for the next push.
- Add a regression test: a failing `streaming_call` keeps the buffer and the flag, and the next `push` retries the full accumulated text. Verified failing before the change, passing after.

Tests: `pytest tests/tts_dashscope_test.py` → 64 passed, 26 subtests passed locally.

title: fix(embedding): deep-copy DashScope multimodal cache identifier
body:
## Why

`_call_multimodal` builds its cache identifier from `api_kwargs` with a shallow comprehension:

```python
cache_identifier = {k: v for k, v in api_kwargs.items() if k != "api_key"}
```

so `cache_identifier["input"]` **is** the same list/dict objects that get passed to `dashscope.MultiModalEmbedding.call`. The SDK's upload preprocessing (`_preprocess_message_inputs` → `check_and_upload`) mutates those elements **in place**: for any local path or `file://` URL it replaces the element value with the freshly minted `oss://` URL (`oss_utils.py`: `contents[i] = file_url ... elem[key] = ...`).

The identifier is hashed at `retrieve()` time (before the call) and again at `store()` time (after the call) — two different payloads, two different SHA-256 filenames. For any input that triggers an upload:

- the cache can never hit, so every call re-uploads and re-embeds;
- each call writes one permanently unreachable `.npy`;
- those dead entries evict *live* ones, because `FileEmbeddingCache._maintain_cache_dir` evicts oldest-mtime-first.

Reachability: `file://` URLSources are a first-class concept across the repo (every chat formatter detects and reads them, and `workspace/_base.py` produces `workspace:///` sources), and `_format_data_block` **requires** `URLSource` for video inputs — so a local video file can only arrive as a `file://` URL, which is precisely the SDK's upload trigger.

Repro:

```python
cache = FileEmbeddingCache(cache_dir=tmp)
m = DashScopeEmbeddingModel(..., model="qwen3-vl-embedding", dimensions=2560, embedding_cache=cache)
blk = DataBlock(source=URLSource(url="file:///C:/vid/a.mp4", media_type="video/mp4"))
await m([blk]); await m([blk])   # 2 API calls, 2 cache files, 0 hits
```

(The text path is safe: `TextEmbedding.call` never rewrites the input list.)

## What

- Deep-copy the cache identifier so `retrieve()` and `store()` hash the same payload regardless of what the SDK does to `api_kwargs` afterwards. The copy is cheap — dict/list shells plus immutable strings.
- Add a regression test simulating the SDK's in-place rewrite (`input[0]["image"] = "oss://uploaded/img.png"` inside the mocked call) and asserting the second identical call hits the cache. Verified failing before the change, passing after.

Tests: `pytest tests/embedding_dashscope_test.py` → 16 passed, 2 subtests passed locally.
